pests.symptoms: Feeding at the base of tillers causes leaves to turn orange-yellow then brown and dry ("hopperburn"), which can kill the plant. Can also transmit rice ragged stunt and rice grassy stunt viruses.
risk_factors: Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides, which kills natural predators and causes hopper population resurgence.
Dense planting and excessive nitrogen fertilization.
Continuous flooded conditions favor hopper survival.
pests.escalation_criteria: More than 3-5 insects per tiller is considered high and warrants closer inspection and possible intervention.

actions.action: Inspect surrounding plants and nearby field areas for additional hopper activity at the base of tillers.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization and overly dense planting, both of which favor hopper buildup.
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticide use; it removes natural predators and parasites and can trigger a larger hopper resurgence.
Capture another field observation within the next monitoring interval to confirm whether hopper activity is spreading.

pests.symptoms: Larvae fold a leaf around themselves, webbing the margins together with silk, and feed inside, producing longitudinal white/transparent streaks on the blade.
risk_factors: Dense planting and excessive nitrogen fertilization.
Presence of grassy weeds in and around the field.
Early-season insecticide use that disrupts natural biological control.
pests.escalation_criteria: Widespread leaf folding across many hills during active tillering/vegetative stage warrants closer inspection.

actions.action: Inspect nearby hills for folded leaves and check whether damage is spreading across the field.
Reduce planting density, use balanced fertilizer rates, and remove grassy weeds from the field and borders.

Early-season insecticide use against leaffolder is generally discouraged: it has little economic benefit at this stage and can disrupt natural pest control, favoring secondary pests such as planthoppers.
Capture another field observation within the next monitoring interval to track whether damage is increasing.

pests.symptoms: Larvae bore into tillers, causing "deadhearts" (drying of the central shoot) during the vegetative stage and "whiteheads" (unfilled, bleached panicles) during the reproductive stage.
risk_factors: One of the most damaging insect pests of rice in Asia; damage can be severe under favorable conditions.
Continuous rice cropping without a fallow/rotation period.
pests.escalation_criteria: Visible deadhearts in the vegetative stage or whiteheads at the reproductive stage warrant field-level inspection and, if extensive, expert consultation.

actions.action: Visually inspect the crop for deadhearts (vegetative stage) or whiteheads (reproductive stage); dissect a few affected stems to confirm larvae or pupae are present.
Where feasible, follow rice with a different crop or a fallow period rather than continuous rice cropping to break the borer's life cycle.
Capture another field observation within the next monitoring interval, focusing on tiller and panicle symptoms.

pests.symptoms: Larvae bore into stalks, tassels, and ears, weakening stalks and reducing yield.
risk_factors: Continuous maize cropping without resistant varieties.
Use of broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupt egg parasitoids (e.g. Trichogramma species).
pests.escalation_criteria: Multiple larvae per plant or extensive stalk/ear tunneling across the field warrants closer inspection.

actions.action: Scout nearby plants for the number of caterpillars per plant and check stalks/tassels/ears for tunneling.
Mechanical removal of tassels has been reported to reduce borer populations; consider this where practical and locally recommended.
Avoid unnecessary synthetic insecticide applications, as they can interfere with natural egg parasitoids (e.g. Trichogramma) that help suppress this pest.

pests.symptoms: Caterpillars feed on leaf tips and margins and, at high populations, can strip whole leaves down to the midrib. Outbreaks can move in large groups between fields.
risk_factors: High populations can build up quickly and move between fields during outbreaks.
Larvae are nocturnal, often feeding at night or on cloudy days, making early detection harder.
pests.escalation_criteria: Rapidly increasing counts across successive observations, or visible leaf-stripping across many plants, warrant urgent inspection given this pest's outbreak/migratory behavior.

actions.action: Inspect nearby plants and field borders for additional armyworm activity; outbreaks can move quickly between fields.
Where applicable at the seedbed stage, flooding is reported as an effective defensive measure against armyworm buildup.
Recheck the field within a short interval, as armyworm populations can increase and spread rapidly during an outbreak.

pests.symptoms: Sap-feeding insects that cluster on leaves, stems, or roots; heavy infestations can weaken plants, though aphids are generally a minor, localized pest in rice.
risk_factors: Loss of natural enemies (predators, parasitoids) due to broad-spectrum insecticide use.
pests.escalation_criteria: Aphids are typically minor and localized; escalate only if colonies are large, spreading rapidly, or found alongside disease symptoms (aphids can vector some plant viruses).

actions.action: Check nearby plants for aphid colonies and note whether natural enemies (e.g. lady beetles, parasitic wasps) are already present.
Favor conserving natural enemies (lady beetles, parasitic wasps, predatory insects) over broad-spectrum insecticide use, since aphids are usually kept in check biologically.
Recheck the area at the next monitoring interval to confirm whether the aphid colony is spreading.

pests.symptoms: Adults chew small, rounded "shot-hole" perforations in leaves, most damaging to seedlings and young transplants.
risk_factors: Newly emerged seedlings and young transplants are most vulnerable.
Weedy field margins and crop residue can harbor overwintering populations.
pests.escalation_criteria: Heavy shot-hole damage on seedlings/young transplants warrants closer, more frequent monitoring since this stage is most vulnerable.

actions.action: Check seedlings and young transplants twice weekly for flea beetle damage until plants are well established.
Remove weeds along field margins and manage crop residue after harvest; consider adjusting planting time to avoid peak adult activity where practical.
Recheck seedlings within a few days, since flea beetle damage is most critical during early plant establishment.

pests.symptoms: Larvae feed on foliage of brassica crops (cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and relatives) and contaminate heads with frass.
risk_factors: Monocropped brassica fields without intercropping tend to see higher pest pressure.
Adults are attracted to light, so light traps can indicate local moth activity.
pests.escalation_criteria: Extensive foliar feeding or frass contamination on marketable heads warrants closer inspection.

actions.action: Check nearby plants for larvae and frass contamination; pheromone/light traps can help time monitoring visits.
Intercropping brassica plantings (rather than large monocrop blocks) has been associated with reduced egg-laying and larval populations of this pest.
Conserve natural enemies where present (parasitic wasps such as Trichogramma and Microplitis species, and parasitic flies), which contribute to control of this pest.

pests.symptoms: Larvae feed on foliage, and at high densities can cause significant defoliation.
risk_factors: Weedy fields attract egg-laying adult moths.
Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides can reduce naturally occurring parasitoids and predators.
pests.escalation_criteria: Escalate if defoliation is extensive or natural biological control is clearly failing to limit population growth.

actions.action: Inspect surrounding plants for larvae and defoliation; treat only if natural (biological) suppression is not keeping populations in check.
Maintain good weed control, since adult moths are attracted to weeds for egg-laying.
Naturally occurring parasitoid wasps, a tachinid fly, and viral diseases often keep this pest at low levels; conserve these natural enemies where possible.

pests.symptoms: Nymphs and adults feed on buds, flowers, and developing fruit/seed structures, which can cause deformed growth or fruit/seed loss.
risk_factors: Weedy field borders, roadways, and ditches support overwintering and spring buildup of this pest.
Flowering cover crops or legumes near the field can drive adult migration into the crop as they senesce.
pests.escalation_criteria: Escalate if adult migration into the field is observed during early crop stages, since this is the period of greatest susceptibility.

actions.action: Scout for adult and nymph activity, especially during early crop growth stages when migration into the field is most likely.
Manage weeds along roadways, ditches, and field borders, and mow or disc cover crops/legumes before they flower, to reduce spring buildup and migration into the field.
Conserve natural enemies (egg and nymphal parasitoids, big-eyed bugs, damsel bugs, minute pirate bugs, spiders), which provide partial control.

pests.symptoms: A highly polyphagous caterpillar pest; larvae feed on foliage across many crops and can cause substantial defoliation at high densities.
risk_factors: Broad host range allows populations to persist across multiple crops/seasons in an area.
Documented resistance development to multiple insecticide classes (organophosphates, carbamates, pyrethroids) from repeated chemical use.
pests.escalation_criteria: Escalate if larvae are in later instars (4th-5th) across many plants, as these are harder to control and cause the most feeding damage.

actions.action: Scout for eggs and early-instar larvae on nearby plants; pheromone traps can help detect adult activity early.
Trap crops (e.g. castor or taro, where locally appropriate) have been shown to draw this pest away from the main crop.
Handpicking is reported as effective specifically against later-instar (4th-5th) larvae, which are otherwise harder to control chemically.
This pest has documented resistance to several common insecticide classes; repeated chemical treatment without rotation is discouraged.

pests.symptoms: Adults chew narrow longitudinal feeding scars on leaves; larvae feed on roots underwater, which can reduce root mass and yield.
risk_factors: Weedy vegetation on levees and field edges near the time of seeding.
Adults concentrate near levees and field edges early in the season.
pests.escalation_criteria: This pest has one generation per year in most systems, so timing of any intervention relative to the adult activity window is critical; escalate if adult scarring is widespread near field edges early in the season.

actions.action: Check field edges and levee-adjacent areas for adult feeding scars, since adults concentrate there early in the season.
Control weedy vegetation on levees and field edges around the time of seeding to reduce infestation pressure.
Recheck field edges at the next monitoring interval; timing matters since this pest typically has only one generation per season.
